newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek PM Simitis subdues farmers but for how long?.
newsitem.headline: Greek PM Simitis subdues farmers but for how long?.

text.p: Greek Prime Minister Costas Simitis has thwarted a second farmers' revolt in three months but his victory could be short-lived if he fails to deal with deep-rooted problems in agriculture, analysts said on Monday.
The soft-spoken techocrat, ignoring pleas from even within his socialist party to soften his stance, stuck to his guns and forced protesting farmers to retreat.
But farmers vowed to return to the highways in March if demands for lower taxes, cheaper fuel, more state subsidies and the settlement of debts are not met soon.
"The farmers' struggle will continue. The government must understand that it's not finished with us. We will continue until the final victory," farmers' representative Yannis Patakis told reporters.
Farmers pulled back some 2,000 tractors lining the main north-south highway in the central Thessaly region after police immobilised them by deflating their tyres.
For several days last week they had eluded police, driving their tractors through vast cotton fields and across rivers to reach key points of the national highway and threaten to cut off traffic.
Political analysts warned that the second round of protests would not be the last unless the government tackled chronic problems in agriculture.

"The farmers' withdrawal from the road network is not a victory for the government because problems in agriculture remain unresolved," the liberal daily Eleftherotypia said in its main editorial. "There is no strategy in agricultural policy."
Simitis, criticised for doing nothing to prevent a 25-day road and rail blockade in December, sent 5,000 police to central Greece with strict orders to keep roads open.

He waited out the crippling December blockade, which brought criticism from some European Union partners, but then -- with little progress in talks with the government -- the farmers returned to the roads on February 4.
Simitis turned down most of their demands, saying strict EU rules and Greece's urgent need to meet its economic targets for monetary union tied his hands.
He refused to bow to farmers' requests to meet him for fear of appearing weak to other groups opposing his strict economic policies.

Since coming to power in September, he has faced an almost constant wave of protests and strikes against his 1997 budget, described as the toughest in 15 years, and his strict incomes and tax policies.
As a last measure, he sent his top ministers and party officials for a tour of the countryside over the weekend to explain the government's position and placate angry farmers.
Some ministers boldly admitted that successive governments had failed to inform farmers of the changes needed to conform with the EU's agricultural policies.
"Not every farmer in Thessaly can continue to grow cotton. Some must switch to other crops," Development Minister Vasso Papandreou said.
Greek farmers, pampered by rich EU handouts during the 1980s, have seen prices fall dramatically in recent years or their produce left to rot.

"The biggest mistake that we are paying for now is that agricultural policy has for years cultivated the false impression that nothing needs to change in our country, while dramatic changes have taken place in other EU countries," said the major daily Ta Nea in an editorial.
